label: explain-track-6
one_line: We test whether a computer-checked rulebook can say if a claimed flying fish glide breaks the laws of physics.
what: We are testing a referee for animal claims. The referee takes a claim, such as "a fish glided 50 metres". It checks the claim against physical rules that a proof program has verified. It gives one of three answers: ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. It never says "proved". Our test case is the flying fish, because its body was measured in a wind tunnel. The newest glide test is a plan with bets written down first. It has no result yet.
why: Claims about animals are often repeated from paper to paper without anyone redoing the sums. When we reopened the sources, almost every number held. But one headline pair of numbers came from two different simulated flights. A referee that checks the arithmetic and says plainly what it cannot judge is useful. It could be used on many other animals. It is also honest about its limits. For example, a long field glide may include paddling on the water, which the simple rule does not cover.

steps.text: Measure the fish. Researchers put stuffed fish models in a wind tunnel running at 12 metres per second. They recorded how much lift and drag the body makes.
steps.picture: Holding a paper plane out of a car window and feeling it pull up and back.

steps.text: Turn the measurements into a speed floor. Using a model fish of 0.06 kilograms, we work out the slowest speed that still holds it up. We get 9.85 metres per second.
steps.picture: A bicycle that wobbles and falls once you go slower than a walking pace.

steps.text: Turn the speed into a distance limit. A fish that starts fast can trade speed for distance, like a cyclist coasting off a hill. The best lift-to-drag ratio found was 4.37.
steps.picture: Coasting downhill: the longer the slope and the faster the start, the farther you roll.

steps.text: Write the rule as a proof. A proof program checks every step of the rule, so no step is trusted on faith.
steps.picture: A strict teacher who marks each line of a sum, not just the final answer.

steps.text: Write down bets before looking. For example, a 10 metres per second launch should buy under 1 metre of level glide. Each bet says what result would count against us.
steps.picture: Writing your guess in a sealed envelope before the race.

steps.text: Re-check the sources. We downloaded the original papers and data and redid the sums with a short program anyone can rerun.
steps.picture: Checking a restaurant bill line by line.

steps.text: Look for rivals. We ask what else could explain long flights, such as the fish paddling its tail on the water surface.
steps.picture: A runner who seems to leap far, but took a running start you did not count.

steps.text: Report the answer in three words only. The referee says ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. "Not ruled out" never means "possible".
steps.picture: A court that can say guilty, not guilty, or not enough evidence, but never "innocent for sure".

wrong_if: We bet that the stall-speed floor and the distance limit hold for a fish that glides with no tail paddling. We would be wrong if a careful, measured, unpowered glide went clearly farther than the limit allows. We would also be wrong if the fish in the wind tunnel could fly slower than 9.85 metres per second. Another bet is that a launch at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second cannot give a long level glide. A measured long glide from such a launch would break it.
could_go_wrong: Every wind tunnel number comes from stuffed fish models, so a live fish may behave differently.
The distance rule only holds when lift equals weight, so a fish that is lofted upward could beat it.
Field distances such as 50 metres are second-hand, and we found no public raw record of real glide tracks.
The simulation paper pairs a 45.4 metre distance with a 13.2 metre height from different runs, so it is easy to misread.
The aquarium paper gives take-off speeds but not how long each leap lasted, so one planned test cannot be done with it.
Paddling on the water may explain long flights, and the simple rule cannot judge those.
Some of our own predictions were found to be unable to fail on their own, so they add less than they seem to.
The proof program checks the logic, but the numbers fed into it can still be wrong or out of date.

questions.a: We reopened the original papers and reran the sums with short programs. Almost all numbers matched. Anyone can rerun them using the commands listed below.
We did not rerun the proof program ourselves for the newest proof. We found no public raw glide-track data. We did not read every figure in the simulation paper.
No. It is a plan with bets written first. We found no results for it yet.

questions.q: Does "not ruled out" mean the claim is true?
questions.a: No. It only means our rules could not knock the claim down.

questions.q: Why would a fish glide farther than the rule allows?
questions.a: It may paddle its tail on the water first, which adds push. The rule leaves that out. So a longer field distance does not mean a law is wrong.

questions.q: How slowly can the model fish fly?
questions.a: About 9.85 metres per second, a little faster than a quick cycling pace. That uses a 0.06 kilogram fish and the best lift number measured in the tunnel.

questions.q: How fast do live fish leap in an aquarium?
questions.a: They were estimated at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second. That is well below the 9.85 floor, but it is a different fish from the model.

questions.q: Why does a simulation headline need care?
questions.a: Its 45.4 metre glide and 13.2 metre height came from two different runs. All the runs began at 20 metres per second.

glossary.plain: Software that checks each step of a maths argument and refuses it if any step is missing.
A tube where fast air blows over a model so we can measure the forces on it.
The upward push that air gives a moving wing or body.
The backward pull of air that slows something moving.
How much lift you get for each unit of drag; a higher number means a farther glide.
The slowest speed at which the wings still hold the animal up.
Moving through the air without flapping or any push.
A computer model that imitates what would happen in real life.
Skimming along the water with the tail beating, which gives extra push.
A glide that stays at about the same height.
Quoted from an older paper rather than measured by the people now reporting it.
A result we write down before looking, so we can later see if we were wrong.
A measure of speed; 10 metres per second is about the pace of a fast cyclist.
A jump out of the water made by a live fish in a tank.
Our name for the checker that tests claims against rules.

left_out: Claim that thrust-supported taxiing is the 'strongest rival': only partly supported, since no source says 'strongest'; it is shown here as one rival, not the strongest.
Claim that only two open datasets exist for gliding animals: the broad negative could not be fully verified, so we say only that we found no public raw glide tracks for fish.
Claim that the newest proof file passed the proof checker with no errors: not rerun by the verifier, so it is not stated as fact.
Claim that law set 1.8.1 itself fixed the wrong flagging of gliding fish: the fix was made in 1.7.0, so no credit is given to 1.8.1.
Exact counts for the fin-size data (49 fish, 14 large) were only partly reproduced, so they are not used.
Several of our own bets were reported as unable to fail independently; this is mostly the author's reading, so it is only mentioned as a general risk.
